# Fault-tolerant interfaces for quantum LDPC codes

Fault-tolerant interfaces for quantum LDPC codes Matthias Christandl1, Omar Fawzi2, and Ashutosh Goswami1 1Department of Mathematical Sciences, University of Copenhagen, Denmark 2Universit ́e de Lyon, Inria, ENS de Lyon, UCBL, LIP, France christandl@math.ku.dk, omar.fawzi@ens-lyon.fr, akg@math.ku.dk

The preparation of a quantum state using a noisy quantum computer (gate noise strength δ) will necessarily affect an O(δ)-fraction of the qubits, no matter which protocol is used. Here, we show that fault-tolerant quantum state preparation can be achieved with constant qubit overhead improving on previous constructions requiring polylogarithmic

To achieve this, we add to the toolbox of fault-tolerant schemes for circuits with quantum input and output. More specifically, we construct fault-tolerant interfaces that decrease the level of protection for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. When information is encoded in multiple code blocks, our interfaces have constant qubit

In our decoder construction that changes the level of protection by an arbitrary amount, we circumvent bottlenecks to error pileup and overhead by gradual lowering of the level of encoding at the same time as we increase the number of blocks on which decoding is carried out simultaneously.

Fault-tolerant quantum computation is typically motivated from the perspective of realizing quantum computations that have classical input and output, e.g. in the computation of a function. One of the main results in the field of fault-tolerant quantum computation is the threshold theorem, which states that any quantum circuit with classical input and output can be performed reliably, using a fault-tolerant circuit, provided that the noise rate is below a constant, i.e., an error rate not depending on the number of locations (gates) in the (original) circuit [AB97; Kit97; Pre98; AGP06]. While the threshold theorem addresses quantum computations with classical input and output, many important quantum information tasks involve using circuits that have quantum input/output. Examples include quantum communication protocols, quantum learning tasks, and, more generally, information processing tasks that involve interactions with black boxes. Such black boxes may have inputs and outputs that are quantum and encoded in a way that we do not control. In such settings, the notion of fault-tolerance must be adapted. In particular, a fault-tolerant implementation must preserve the original circuit’s input/output relation in the encoding fixed by the black boxes. As the quantum inputs and outputs are affected by noise, the natural guarantee to aim for is that the fault-tolerant circuit realizes the original one up to a weak noise applied on input and output systems.

A framework for fault-tolerant circuits with quantum input/output was presented in Ref. [CFG26] based on the fault-tolerance formalism of [Kit97]. This framework builds on the fault-tolerance literature and unifies and improves on previous specific results such as state preparation circuits [Got14] and preparation and measurement interfaces [CM22; BCM24]. The framework was used to construct a constant qubit overhead fault-tolerant scheme for general noise [CFG25] and to construct a fault-tolerant QRAM [Dal+25]. An important primitive in fault-tolerant quantum input/output is the fault-tolerant preparation of an n-qubit quantum state described by a circuit. This primitive was achieved in [Got14; CM22; BCM24; CFG26] using concatenated codes and thus incurs a qubit overhead that grows polylogarithmically with n. In this work, we ask whether it is possible to achieve fault-tolerant realization of state preparation circuits, with constant qubit overhead. It is worth emphasizing that the faulttolerant circuit must preserve the same input-output relation as the original circuit, i.e., it should prepare the target state up to a weak noise acting on it, rather than an encoded version of that state in a quantum error-correcting code. We answer this question positively in the model of circuit-level stochastic noise, where the noise acts independently on each gate. The noisy version of a gate g, under circuit-level stochastic noise with error rate δ ∈ [0, 1], realizes the gate g with probability (1 − δ), while with probability δ, it realizes an arbitrary quantum gate ̃g with the same input and output

In our first main result, we show that any state preparation circuit can be realized faulttolerantly up to a local stochastic noise, while incurring only a constant qubit overhead. Our state preparation is according to the following theorem. Theorem 1 (Informal version of Theorem 44). There exists a threshold value δth > 0 and a constant κ > 0 such that the following holds. Consider a state preparation circuit Φ, with x qubit output and operating on O(x) qubits and having size |Φ| = poly(x). Then, there exists a quantum circuit Φ, with the same input and output systems as Φ and working on O(x) qubits, such that its noisy realization ̃TΦ under circuit level stochastic noise with parameter δ < δth approximately simulates Φ up to a layer of local stochastic noise with strength δ′ = O(δκ) applied at the output. In order to establish this result, we consider quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. The reason for this is as follows: first, they encode logical qubits at constant rate, i.e., with a constant qubit overhead, and have good error correction performance and efficient decoders [TZ13; LTZ15; FGL18; BE21a; BE21b]. Moreover, there are families of QLDPC codes with a minimum distance scaling linearly with the code length [LZ22; PK22]. Second, a constant qubit overhead scheme for fault-tolerant computation has been constructed using QLDPC codes [Got14; FGL20; CFG25]. Moreover, progress in recent years has made QLDPC codes a leading path towards fault-tolerant quantum computing [Yod+25; He+25; Cro+24; Xu+25; Bon+25; WSC25; Web+26]. We construct a decoding interface circuit, which fault-tolerantly maps logical information encoded in multiple blocks of a QLDPC code into bare physical qubits, up to a local stochastic noise. Moreover, if the number of blocks is sufficiently large, the qubit overhead of the decoding interface circuit is constant. Our decoding interface, which is crucial for faulttolerant state preparation in Theorem 1, is as follows.

Theorem 2 (Informal version of Theorem 25). For certain families of QLDPC codes Cr, r = 1, 2, . . . , where Cr encodes mr logical qubits in nr physical qubits, the following holds. There exists a polynomial p(·), constants μ, κ > 0 and a threshold value δth > 0, such that for all encoding levels r, quantum information encoded in h blocks of Cr can be decoded into bare physical qubits with a decoding interface circuit affected by circuit-level stochastic noise of strength δ < δth. The error on the output is a local stochastic channel with strength δ′ = O(δκ) if the input has at most μnr errors in each block. The qubit overhead of the decoding interface is constant for h ≥ p(mr). We emphasize that our methods to obtain Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are significantly different from methods used in [Got14] to obtain constant qubit overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing. In fact, a straightforward generalization of the protocols in [Got14] will not lead to a fault-tolerant decoding interface. To highlight this difference, we below first describe the construction due to [Got14] and outline the challenges in generalizing it to state preparation circuits. We then present our own construction and highlight the main innovations. Description of Gottesman’s constant qubit overhead scheme for quantum computation: The fault-tolerant construction in [Got14] considers sequential circuits, such that at any layer only one or a few non-trivial gates are applied on a selected set of logical qubits, while the idle gate is applied on the remaining logical qubits. Any quantum circuit Φ, operating on x′ qubits, can be turned into a sequential circuit Φseq by incurring only a O(x′) overhead in the size (i.e., total number of locations) and depth of the circuit. We note that this sequentialization is key to ensuring constant qubit overhead. Consider the sequential circuit Φseq, operating on x′ logical qubits. Consider a QLDPC code family Cr, r = 1, . . . , encoding mr logical qubits in nr physical qubits such that the encoding rate mr nr is constant. We first divide x′ logical qubits into h = x′ mr blocks, each containing mr logical qubits. For the fault-tolerant circuit ΦFT, we encode each block of mr logical qubits in a code block of QLDPC code Cr, containing nr physical qubits. We replace a layer of gates in Φseq by a logical layer in ΦFT as follows: If the idle gate is applied on a block in Φseq, we apply the error correction on the corresponding block in ΦFT. If a non-trivial gate is applied on some of the qubits in a block in Φseq, we apply the corresponding logic gate on the corresponding block in ΦFT. A logic gate on a QLDPC code block is applied using gate teleportation technique on the corresponding logical block [Got14; FGL20; Gro19]. The error correction circuit for QLDPC codes operates on O(mr) qubits; therefore, the qubit overhead of ΦECr is constant for the blocks on which error correction is applied. However, for the logic gate implementation using gate teleportation, the overhead is not constant with respect to the block on which it is applied. But since we only need one non-trivial gate, by choosing mr to be sub-linearly growing with x′, for example mr = √ x′, the total overhead can be made constant with respect to the total number of qubits x′. Challenges in generalizing constant qubit overhead scheme to state preparation: As mentioned before, we need a decoding interface to extend constant qubit overhead scheme to state preparation. We note that in principle, a teleportation based decoding interface can be obtained using teleportation as depicted in Fig 1. Let Vr be the encoding isometry of Cr

Based on the two classical outcomes of the Bell measurement a Pauli correction P is applied to the remaining half of |Ψr⟩. mapping mr qubits into nr qubits. One can teleport any code state of Cr out of the code space by using the entangled state

(i) the teleportation-based interface is not fault-tolerant itself, (ii) the sequentialization procedure is not robust for the decoding interface. We first describe challenge (i). We note that teleportation involves logical Bell measurement on two code blocks of the code Cr (see Fig. 1). Logical Bell measurements correspond to transversal Bell measurements on physical qubits of the two code blocks [Gro19, Chapter 6]. The outcome of the physical Bell measurements are further classically processed to get the outcome of logical Bell measurement, based on which a Pauli correction is applied on the teleported, unencoded state. The main obstacle here is that the time complexity of this classical processing depends on the code length nr of Cr. For QLDPC codes, the algorithms for classical processing scale O(polylog(nr)) [FGL18; Gro19; Gu+24; LZ23]. This implies that teleported unencoded qubits need to wait for O(polylog(nr)) time steps. Since there is no active error correction on the unencoded qubits, the quantum information will eventually be garbled up as r → ∞. We emphasize that for a fixed r, the waiting time is not a problem as long as δ is sufficiently small; the problem arises only when considering a sequence of codes Cr, r = 1, 2, . . . , and a

We note that the teleportation based interface does not have a constant qubit overhead due to fault-tolerant preparation of the state |Ψr⟩, which is done using concatenated codes as in gate teleportation. We now consider challenge (ii). We suppose that there is an interface circuit Γr (not necessarily using teleportation) that maps logical information encoded in Cr onto bare physical qubits fault-tolerantly (i.e., up to a weak noise on the output), but requires a qubit overhead that grows with nr, i.e., the number of physical qubits in Cr. Suppose further that we want to upgrade the interface

Each horizontal wire represents either a block of nr qubits or a block of mr qubits as written on top of the wire. In the first layer, Γr is applied on the first wire mapping nr qubits to mr qubits. While Γr is being applied on the first wire, error correction steps are applied on the remaining wires. Similarly, on jth layer for j ≤ h, where h is the total number of wires, Γr is applied on the jth wire, and on all the wires before it i = 1, . . . , j − 1, idle gates are applied and on all the wires after it i = j + 1, . . . , h error correction steps are applied. to a constant qubit overhead interface using sequentialization technique used for logic gate implementation in Gottesman’s scheme. As depicted in Fig. 2, we consider h code blocks of Cr, and apply the interface Γr on only one (or a few) of the chosen blocks in a layer, and continue in this way until the interface has been applied on all h blocks. We choose the code parameter r such that mr grows sub-linearly with respect to x′, i.e., the total number of logical qubits. This in turn implies that h = x′ mr grows (i.e., not constant) with respect to x′. This sequentialization procedure does not lead to a fault-tolerant decoding interface, as we now explain: Once the decoding interface is applied on a block, the logical qubits therein are not anymore protected by the code. However, such an unprotected block needs to wait until the interface has been applied on the remaining blocks. Since h is growing with x′, the unprotected block of mr qubits needs to wait for t time steps that grows with x′ for the remaining blocks to complete. As t is not constant, the logical information encoded in the unprotected block will be completely lost as x′ → ∞. We now present our construction. Fault-tolerant decoding interface with constant qubit overhead: Consider h code blocks of Cr. Instead of mapping the information completely out of a given code block, we consider a partial decoding interface Γr,r−1, which maps logical qubits encoded in one block of Cr into two blocks of Cr−1. The interface Γr,r−1 is based on teleportation; therefore, requires

Figure 3: constant qubit overhead interface: sequential application of the partial interfaces Γr−y,r−y−1 for y = 0, 1, 2 and h = 4. As the level decreases from r to r −1 to r −2, the number of blocks increases (4, 8, 16), and the fraction of blocks on which the interface is applied in parallel (shaded) also grows (1/4, 1/2, 3/4). fault-tolerant preparation of an entangled resource state. Hence, Γr,r−1 does not have a constant qubit overhead. We note that the interface Γr,r−1 avoids challenge (i) from above since the teleported information is still encoded in the code space of Cr−1 on which error correction is applied while the classical processing is done on physical Bell measurements. To achieve constant qubit overhead, we consider a different sequentialization procedure as explained below (see also Fig. 3). Consider h blocks of Cr. To keep the overhead constant, we choose a small fraction of blocks of Cr on which the circuit Γr,r−1 is applied in parallel, while performing error correction on the remaining blocks. This procedure is repeated until Γr,r−1 has been applied on all h blocks, after which we obtain 2h blocks of Cr−1. Since Γr−1,r−2 has a smaller qubit overhead than Γr,r−1, we may choose a larger fraction of blocks on which to apply Γr−1,r−2 in parallel, and repeat it until Γr−1,r−2 has been applied on all the blocks. Iterating the above procedure, we decrease the level of QLDPC code through sequence r, r − 1, r − 2, . . . . The fraction of blocks on which Γr−y,r−y−1 is applied in parallel increases with y; hence the processing time at level r − y, i.e., time it takes to apply Γr−y,r−y−1 on all 2yh blocks, decreases with y = 0, 1, 2, . . . . This property is crucial for fault-tolerance since the logical error rate of Cr−y increases with y and the decreasing processing time prevents errors from accumulating excessively. We stop the iteration r, r − 1, r − 2, . . . , at some fixed level r′. Since r′ is fixed, we can map from level r′ to 1 by applying Γr′ on all the blocks in parallel, and only blowing up the overhead by a constant factor. It is worth emphasizing that fault-tolerant state preparation and decoding interface with constant qubit overhead have several potential applications. We remark on these applications in fault-tolerant computation and communication in Section 6.2.

Structure of manuscript The manuscript is structured as follows. After some preliminary notation, which is presented in Section 2, we discuss properties of QLDPC codes in Section 3. In Section 4, we present and discuss our main results on fault-tolerant interfaces. The error analysis of the interfaces will be presented in a separate section, Section 5. In Section 6, we derive constant qubit overhead fault-tolerant state preparation and discuss its applications. Related work We note that in independent concurrent work, constructions in the faulttolerant quantum input/output paradigm have been developed using constant rate concatenated codes [BY26].

Notation. We denote the single-qubit Hilbert space by C2. The set of linear operators on C2 is denoted by L(C2). Quantum channels are denoted by calligraphic letters such as N , T , V, W, U , etc. For any positive integer n, we write [n] := {1, . . . , n}. We shall denote the identity operator as 1 and identity channel as I. In the following, we recall necessary background on quantum error correcting codes and noise models in the context of fault-tolerant quantum computing. In the last subsection, we recall a recent statement on fault-tolerant state preparation, with a growing qubit overhead

Quantum codes: A quantum code C of type (n, m), that is, encoding m logical qubits in n physical qubits is defined by an isometry V : (C2)⊗m → (C2)⊗n, embedding m qubit Hilbert space into n qubit Hilbert space. The Im(V ) ⊆ (C2)⊗n is referred to as the corresponding code space. In this work, we will consider a particular family of quantum codes called Calderbank- Shor-Steane (CSS) codes, which are a subset of a larger family of codes known as stabilizer codes [Got97; CS96; Ste96]. Subsystem codes. A subsystem code divides the encoded degrees of freedom into logical qubits, which store the protected quantum information, and gauge qubits, whose state is irrelevant [Bac06; Kri+06]. More precisely, the code space admits a decomposition HL ⊗ HG, where HL and HG correspond to the logical and gauge subsystems, respectively. A subsystem stabilizer code can be obtained from a stabilizer code encoding m logical qubits by declaring l < m of these qubits to be the gauge qubits. We call these code stabilizer

Note that the logical operators that act non-trivially on the logical subsystem, possibly also acting on the gauge subsystems, form a subset of N (S) \ S, where S is the stabilizer group of the original code and N (S) is its normalizer. In this section, we describe the models of quantum circuits and noise used in this paper. We assume a stochastic circuit noise model, where each gate is independently affected by noise. For the purpose of error correction, however, we adopt the more general framework of local stochastic noise channels, which may introduce correlated errors across multiple qubits. This choice reflects the fact that stochastic circuit noise can induce correlated errors on qubits depending on the structure of the circuit.

We work in the circuit model of quantum computation, with a finite gate set A consisting of an idle gate, initialization and measurement in the computational (Pauli-Z) basis, a universal set of unitary gates (e.g., CNOT, Hadamard H, and T ), and their corresponding classically controlled versions. For any gate g ∈ A, we denote by Tg the quantum channel realized by g. We shall consider the following definition of quantum circuit [Kit97; CFG26].

(1) A sequence of finite sets ∆0, . . . , ∆d, called layers. The zeroth layer ∆0 is called the input of the circuit, and the final layer ∆d is the output. Each layer ∆i (for i = 0, . . . , d) decomposes as ∆i = ∆c i ∪∆q i , where ∆c i contains classical wires and ∆q i contains quantum wires. If the circuit has only classical input, then ∆q 0 = ∅; if the circuit has no input, then ∆0 = ∅. We say Φ operates on xq qubits and xc bits, where xq := max{|∆q i |}d i=0 and xc := max{|∆c i |}d i=0. (13) (2) Partitions of each set ∆i−1, i = 1, . . . , d into ordered subsets (registers) Ai1, . . . , Aisi , and a corresponding partition of a superset ∆′ i ⊇ ∆i into registers A′ i1, . . . , A′ isi . (3) A collection of gates gij , where j ≤ si, drawn from the gate set A, such that register Aij and A′ ij are input and outputs of gij , respectively. The gate gij or their numbers (i, j) are called the locations of the quantum circuit. Note that for a fixed i, 1 ≤ i ≤ d, the set of locations {gij : 1 ≤ j ≤ sj } corresponds to the locations in a single layer of

We consider the following noise model for quantum circuits. Definition 11 (Stochastic circuit-level noise). Consider a quantum gate g, realizing quantum channel Tg. The noisy version of the gate g under the stochastic circuit-level noise with parameter δ > 0 realizes the following channel,

where Z is an arbitrary quantum channel, with the same input and output systems as Tg. For our constant qubit overhead protocols, we consider quantum low-density parity-check (quantum LDPC or QLDPC) codes of CSS type [MMM04; BE21b]. We require QLDPC codes to satisfy some additional properties, including constant encoding rate, linear minimum distance, and having efficient error correction protocols. We show that such QLDPC codes can be obtained using quantum Tanner codes [LZ22], and decoder analyses of [LZ23; Gu+24]. 3.1 Rates of QLDPC codes Below, we first provide definition of QLDPC codes. Definition 20 (QLDPC codes). Let Cr, r = 1, 2, . . . be a family of stabilizer codes, where Cr is a code. It is said to be QLDPC if there exists a generating set G, possibly redundant in the sense that it’s not a linearly independent set, such that weight of each g ∈ G is bounded by a constant independent of r and the total number of generators non-trivially acting on any given qubit is upper bounded by a constant independent of the parameter r. For a CSS code family Cr, r = 1, 2, . . . , QLDPC property can be stated in terms of the check matrices of the code. Let H r X and H r Z be the X and Z type parity check matrices of Cr, respectively. Then, the code family is said to be QLDPC if the Hamming weight of any row or column of the parity check matrices H r X and H r Z is constant, i.e., independent of r. Several constructions of QLDPC codes with constant rate and minimum distance growing sub-linearly have been proposed, for instance [TZ13; CDZ13; EKZ22; HHO21]. The existence of QLDPC codes with linear minimum distance remained an open problem for many years, which was settled in Refs. [PK22; LZ22], where the existence of such codes is explicitly

We will not do gauge fixing, i.e., the parity check matrices of the subsystem code are the same as those of Cr. Moreover, we will use the same error correction procedure as Cr for the subsystem code, i.e., the same stabilizer generators and classical decoding procedure as the original code. Thus, the subsystem code inherits the QLDPC stabilizer checks and the error-correction procedure of Cr. The logical Pauli operators associated with the gauge qubits are not used as generators, hence, they are not required to have bounded weight. In the fault-tolerant setting, syndrome extraction is noisy; therefore, faults in the syndrome extraction circuit can introduce additional errors on the physical qubits of the code block and, crucially, can also corrupt the syndrome bits. The goal of fault-tolerant error correction, however, is not to eliminate all errors, but to ensure that, despite noisy

syndrome extraction, the error on the code state remains controlled. In particular, since our QLDPC codes can correct a constant fraction of errors, it suffices that fault-tolerant error correction keeps the physical qubit error below this constant fraction. While many constructions of fault-tolerant error correction rely on multiple rounds of syndrome measurement, some code families admit single-shot fault-tolerant error correction, requiring only one round of noisy syndrome extraction. For quantum Tanner codes, our main candidate family in this paper (see Section 3.1), single-shot fault-tolerant error correction was established in Ref. [Gu+24]. Provided that (i) the input error is within a constant fraction and (ii) the syndrome-bit errors are themselves bounded by a constant fraction, the construction of Ref. [Gu+24] guarantees that the post-correction error on the code state remains within (slightly smaller) constant fraction. A key property of QLDPC codes is that they admit constant-depth syndrome-extraction circuits, since their parity-check matrices have constant-weight rows and columns. Therefore, in the syndrome extraction circuit, a single fault can affect only O(1) data qubits and corrupt only O(1) syndrome bits. Consequently, under circuit-level stochastic noise with a fixed constant parameter, the total error introduced during a round of noisy syndrome extraction has weight with high probability at most a constant fraction of the data qubits and a constant fraction of the syndrome bits (see also [CFG25, Lemma 2]). Combining this property of syndrome extraction with the single-shot fault-tolerant error correction of Ref. [Gu+24] motivates the following definition of fault-tolerant error correction (see also [CFG25, Theorem 5]), which we will use throughout this work. Definition 23 (Fault-tolerant error correction). A quantum circuit ΦECr , with nr qubit input and output, implementing error correction on the code Cr is said to be fault-tolerant if it is of constant depth O(1) and requires O(mr) ancilla qubits, and the following holds for a fixed threshold value δth > 0 and some constants β1, β2, κ, c, c′ > 0: Let N : L((C2)⊗hnr ⊗ R) → L((C2)⊗hnr ⊗ R), with R being a reference system, be an arbitrary quantum channel with stabilizer-reduced weight |N |red ≤ β1nr + β2nr, with respect to each nr qubit system in its input.3 Then, the noisy realization ̃TΦECr of ΦECr under circuit-level stochastic noise with parameter δ < δth applied in parallel to h blocks of Cr gives

In this section, we construct fault-tolerant decoding interfaces with constant qubit overhead for QLDPC codes. Our construction assumes QLDPC code Cr, r = 1, 2, . . . , satisfying Eq. (45)-(46). Moreover, efficient classical decoding and fault-tolerant error correction according to Def. 23 are assumed. As shown in Section 3, quantum Tanner codes combined with the decoder analysis of Refs. [LZ23; Gu+24] satisfy these assumptions. This section is organized as follows: In Section 4.1, we state our main result on the fault-tolerant decoding interface Ξ[h] r , which relies on the fault-tolerance of partial decoding interfaces Γr,r′ . The remaining sections are dedicated to proving this result: In Section 4.2, we discuss the partial decoding interface and in Section 4.4 we provide its error analysis. Section 4.5 provides an extension to multiple code blocks. In Section 4.6 we present the main argument regarding the constant qubit overhead. The error analysis is more involved and will be provided in a separate Section 5.

Our goal is to construct a decoding interface circuit Ξ[h] r that maps mrh logical qubits encoded in h blocks of Cr to bare physical qubits for any r > 0, while having a constant qubit overhead, i.e. operating on O(mrh) qubits. Moreover, for fault-tolerance, we require that the noisy version of Ξ[h] r preserves the logical information encoded in h blocks of Cr up to a weak local stochastic noise applied on the bare physical qubits. Our main result is the following Theorem 25, where we provide our fault-tolerant decoding interfaces for QLDPC codes.
